common_name: Punchline Bearded Iris (Plum Brown and Violet Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Punchline is a mid-20th-century Tall Bearded iris later used as a parent of the Dykes Medal-winning Border Bearded iris 'Brown Lasso'.

directions: Hybridized by Gordon Plough and registered in 1967, Punchline is a Tall Bearded iris carrying blended plum-brown standards over campanula-violet falls edged in a wide, rich reddish-brown border around a rich orangy-yellow beard, giving each bloom a warm, layered autumnal look. It flowers over an unusually long early-to-late season on 34-inch stems. Eugene Buckles later crossed Punchline with a seedling of 'Wild Mustang' and 'Milestone' to produce 'Brown Lasso', the first Border Bearded iris to win the American Dykes Medal, in 1981. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering vigorous.
sources: Iris Wiki / Historic Iris Preservation Society

common_name: Milestone Bearded Iris (Butterscotch-Gold and Dahlia Purple Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Milestone is a mid-20th-century Tall Bearded iris later used as a breeding grandparent of the Dykes Medal-winning Border Bearded iris 'Brown Lasso'.

directions: Hybridized by Gordon Plough from a cross of 'Rainbow Gold' and 'Whole Cloth' and registered in 1964, Milestone is a Tall Bearded iris with rich butterscotch-gold standards over dahlia-purple falls marked with an electric-blue blaze beneath an Indian-yellow beard, styles finished in gold with a lavender midrib. It blooms on 35-inch stems over an early-to-late season. A cross between Milestone and 'Wild Mustang' produced the seedling that, combined with 'Punchline', became 'Brown Lasso', the 1981 American Dykes Medal-winning Border Bearded iris. Divide every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.
sources: Iris Wiki / Historic Iris Preservation Society

common_name: Crystal Gazer Bearded Iris (Ruffled Violet-Blue Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Crystal Gazer is a Keith Keppel Tall Bearded iris later used as a parent of the Dykes Medal-winning 'Florentine Silk'.

directions: Hybridized by Keith Keppel from a cross of 'Lotus Land' and 'Fogbound' and registered in 2002, Crystal Gazer is a ruffled, lightly laced Tall Bearded iris with medium violet-blue standards paling toward the edges, light violet-blue style arms, and blue-lilac falls that pale to a silvery lilac-white center around a lilac-lavender beard tinged soft ibis pink in the throat. It received an Honorable Mention in 2004 and an Award of Merit in 2006 from the American Iris Society. Keppel later used a Crystal Gazer sibling seedling alongside 'Poem of Ecstasy' to breed 'Florentine Silk', the 2012 American Dykes Medal winner. Divide every three to four years after bloom.
sources: Iris Wiki / Historic Iris Preservation Society

common_name: Poem of Ecstasy Bearded Iris (Peach-Pink and Lavender Reblooming Tall Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Poem of Ecstasy is a Wister Medal-winning Tall Bearded iris later used as a parent of the Dykes Medal-winning 'Florentine Silk'.

directions: Bred by Ben Hager and registered in 1995, Poem of Ecstasy is a fluted, ruffled Tall Bearded iris with clear peach-pink standards over smooth, deep lavender falls beneath soft tangerine beards, carrying up to eight buds per 36-inch stem and an occasional light fall rebloom in favorable climates. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1999, an Award of Merit in 2001, and the American Iris Society's Wister Medal in 2004. Keith Keppel later crossed a seedling incorporating Poem of Ecstasy with a 'Crystal Gazer' sibling to breed 'Florentine Silk', the 2012 American Dykes Medal winner. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: Iris Wiki / Historic Iris Preservation Society

common_name: Joan Evans False Freesia (White Freesia laxa Selection with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; in zones 8-10 corms can also go in during fall and are usually left in the ground year-round.

directions: Joan Evans is a distinct selection of the South African corm Freesia laxa (long sold as Anomatheca laxa or Lapeirousia laxa), bearing small white flowers marked with a dramatic dark-red eye at the base of each petal, clearly set apart from both the species' typical scarlet-red blooms and the plain white form sold alongside it. Grassy, iris-like foliage emerges in late winter to early spring ahead of loose sprays of flowers carried on wiry stems into summer. It offsets quickly into a small, fast-spreading clump and self-sows readily in favorable sites, making it a good choice for the front of a woodland border or a lightly shaded rock garden where it can naturalize without becoming aggressive. Grow in dry-ish soil with part sun to part shade and divide congested clumps after several years if flowering declines.

common_name: Coronet Black Currant (Blister-Rust-Resistant Early-Ripening Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring, or in fall in mild climates; Coronet is self-fertile but does not effectively cross-pollinate its siblings 'Consort' or 'Crusader', so pair it with an unrelated black currant if a second cultivar is wanted nearby.

directions: Coronet was bred at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva alongside 'Consort' and 'Crusader' to carry resistance to white pine blister rust, the fungal disease that led many US states to restrict or ban Ribes cultivation for much of the 20th century. It ripens its medium-sized, glossy black berries earlier than many other rust-resistant cultivars, and while the flavor is a touch more bitter than dessert-type European black currants, it processes well into jam, syrup, and cassis. Plants are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 10 to 20 pounds of fruit once established. Prune out canes older than three years each dormant season, since black currants fruit mainly on one- and two-year-old wood.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Rust-Resistant Black Currant Cultivars
